title: Rome and the Protestants agree in words that fallen free choice can do nothing without grace, yet speak differently of it
source_text: THESIS I. THESIBUS ante editis ostendimus Scholae Romanae Doctores cum Protestantibus in eo, verbis saltem, consentire, quod in statu Naturae Lapsae liberum hominis Arbitrium, sine Gratia Christi nihil omnino possit, in iis quae ad veram pietatem pertinent, & per se aeternae saluti conducunt: & tamen, quum Liberum hominis lapsi Arbitrium consideratur respectu boni salutaris & spiritualis, Doctores Scholae Romanae non eodem modo de illo cum Protestantibus loquuntur.
pass_a_gloss: THESIS I. In theses previously published we showed that the Doctors of the Roman School agree with the Protestants in this, at least in words, that in the state of Fallen Nature the free Choice of man, without the Grace of Christ, can do nothing at all, in those things which pertain to true piety, and of themselves conduce to eternal salvation: and yet, when the free Choice of fallen man is considered in respect of saving and spiritual good, the Doctors of the Roman School do not speak of it in the same way with the Protestants.
pass_b_english: Our earlier theses established a verbal agreement, at any rate, between Rome's doctors and the Protestants: once nature has fallen, a man's free choice achieves nothing whatever apart from Christ's grace where true piety and the things that of themselves lead to eternal salvation are concerned.
But when they turn to fallen man's free choice as it stands toward saving, spiritual good, Rome's doctors and the Protestants use different language.

in respect of saving and spiritual good

choices.why: The faculty of free decision; 'free choice' throughout, with 'freedom' for libertas.
